lessons.title: At the station
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Mia are at the train station buying tickets and checking the board.

items.example: Our train is on platform two.
items.note: Say 'platform' for the place where you wait for and get on your train.

image.describe: a friendly cat with a small suitcase standing on a train station platform next to yellow safety lines

items.example: Can I have a single ticket to London, please?
items.note: Ask for a 'single ticket' when you only want to travel one way.

image.describe: a cat paw holding a paper train ticket with one arrow pointing forward

items.example: I would like a return ticket for tomorrow.
items.note: Ask for a 'return ticket' when you want to travel there and come back again.

items.example: Look at the timetable board to see our platform.
items.note: Check the 'timetable board' at the station to see train times and platforms.

items.example: The train is delayed because of bad weather.
items.note: Use 'delayed' when a train or plane is late and leaves after its planned time.

items.example: Our morning train is cancelled today.
items.note: Use 'cancelled' when a train or plane will not go at all.

grammar.title: Tickets and platforms
grammar.explanation: Use 'a single ticket' for one way and 'a return ticket' for going and coming back. Use 'on' before a platform number: 'on platform three'.
examples: I would like a return ticket, please.
The train is on platform five.

practice.prompt: Where do you stand at the station to get on a train?
practice.explanation: You wait on the platform to get on your train.

Can I have a return ticket, please?
Can I have two tickets, please?
practice.explanation: A single ticket is for to go there.

practice.prompt: Mia is coming back tomorrow. Complete her sentence.
practice.text: I would like a ___ for tomorrow.
practice.explanation: Use a return ticket when you are coming back.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: A single ticket goes one way, a return ticket goes both ways, and the timetable board shows times.

practice.prompt: Smarty wants to check the train times. Build the sentence.
practice.explanation: Look at the timetable board to check train times and platforms.

practice.prompt: Your train leaves at four o'clock, but now it leaves at five o'clock. What is the train?
practice.explanation: Delayed means the train is late, not stopped completely.

practice.prompt: There is no train today because of heavy snow. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: The train is ___ today.
practice.explanation: Cancelled means the train will not run at all.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: Our train is on platform three.
practice.answer: Our train is on platform three.
practice.explanation: Use 'on' before a platform number.

lessons.title: On the train
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Leo are inside the train carriage finding their seats and storing luggage.

items.example: I have a seat reservation next to the window.
items.note: Say 'seat reservation' when you booked a specific seat before getting on the train.

image.describe: a small digital screen above a train seat showing a green checkmark and a seat number

items.example: We have to change trains at the next station.
items.note: Use 'change trains' when you get off one train and get on another to finish your trip.

items.example: Keep your suitcase on the luggage rack above your seat.
items.note: The 'luggage rack' is the shelf above the seats where you keep suitcases.

image.describe: a brown cat lifting a blue suitcase onto an overhead luggage rack inside a train carriage

items.example: The next stop is the city museum.
items.note: Say 'the next stop' for the very next station where the train will stop.

items.example: Good news! Our train is running on time.
items.note: Say 'on time' when a train is not late and follows its schedule.

items.example: This is a direct train, so we do not change trains.
items.note: A 'direct train' takes you all the way to your destination without changing trains.

practice.prompt: Someone is sitting in the seat you booked. What do you show them?

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.

practice.answer: Keep your suitcase on the luggage rack.

Keep your suitcase under the table.
Keep your suitcase on the platform.

practice.prompt: This train does not go all the way to Oxford. Complete the sentence.

practice.explanation: You change trains when you get off one train and take another.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: A direct train needs no changes, on time means not late, and the next stop is the coming station.

practice.prompt: Leo is happy because they do not need to get off early. Build the sentence.
practice.explanation: A direct train goes straight to your destination.

practice.prompt: Smarty looks out the train window as the train slows down. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Get your suitcase ready for ___.
practice.explanation: Get ready before the next stop so you do not miss your station.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: Our train is on time now.
practice.answer: Our train is on time now.
practice.explanation: On time means the train is running on schedule.

lessons.title: Future plans
lessons.canDo: Use will and going to for travel
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Zara are planning their weekend trip and checking the weather.

items.example: Hurry up! We are about to get on the train.
items.note: Say 'We are about to' for something that will happen in the very next moment.

items.example: I will probably buy a sandwich on the train.
items.note: Use 'I will probably' when you think something will happen, but you are not completely sure.

items.example: We are leaving at eight o'clock tomorrow morning.
items.note: Use 'We are leaving at' to talk about a fixed travel time on your plan.

items.example: Look at those dark clouds! It is going to rain.
items.note: Say 'It is going to rain' when you see clouds or signs of rain coming soon.

items.example: I will call you when we get to the station.
items.note: Say 'I will call you' to make a quick promise to phone someone later.

items.example: I have decided to take the early train.
items.note: Use 'I have decided to' when you have made a clear choice about your plans.

grammar.title: Talking about future travel
grammar.explanation: Use 'be about to' for something happening right now. Use 'We are leaving at...' for fixed schedules. Use 'going to' for signs you can see now (like rain clouds), and 'will' for promises or things you think will happen.
examples: We are leaving at nine o'clock.
I will call you from the platform.

practice.prompt: The train doors are closing in five seconds. What does Smarty say?
practice.explanation: Use 'We are about to' for something happening right away.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: We are leaving at seven o'clock.
practice.answer: We are leaving at seven o'clock.
options: We are leaving at seven o'clock.
We are leaving at ten o'clock.
I have decided to stay home.
practice.explanation: Use 'We are leaving at' for a fixed departure time.

practice.prompt: The sky is dark and cloudy. Take an umbrella! Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Look outside! ___ soon.
practice.explanation: Use 'It is going to rain' when you see dark clouds.

practice.prompt: Match each phrase with when to use it.
practice.explanation: Use 'I will call you' for promises, 'I will probably' when unsure, and 'I have decided to' for you have decided.

practice.prompt: Zara chose to travel by train instead of by bus. Build the sentence.
practice.answer: I have decided to go by train.
practice.explanation: I have decided to shows a firm plan.

practice.prompt: Smarty is not completely sure where he will sit. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: ___ sit next to the window.
practice.explanation: Use 'I will probably' when something is likely but not certain.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: I will call you tomorrow morning.
practice.answer: I will call you tomorrow morning.
practice.explanation: Use 'I will call you' to promise a phone call.

lessons.title: Movement
lessons.scenario: Smarty gives walking directions from the station to the city museum.

items.example: Go across the park to get to the station.
items.note: Use 'across' when you move from one side to the other side of an open space or bridge.

items.example: The train goes through the forest and the mountain.
items.note: Use 'through' when you move inside something like a tunnel, door, or forest.

items.example: We walked along the river in the afternoon.
items.note: Use 'along' when you follow a line like a river, beach, or long platform.

items.example: Turn left and go towards the museum.
items.note: Use 'towards' when you move in the direction of a place or person.

items.example: Go past the supermarket and stop at the corner.
items.note: Use 'past' when you go right by a building without stopping there.

items.note: Use 'out of' when you move from inside a building or train to the outside.

grammar.title: Prepositions of movement
grammar.explanation: Prepositions of movement show direction: 'out of' (inside to outside), 'across' (one side to the other), 'through' (inside a space like a park or door), 'along' (following a river or platform), 'past' (going by a place), and 'towards' (in the direction of).
examples: Go out of the door and across the park.
Run along the river past the café.

practice.prompt: You are inside the station and want to go outside. Which words fit?
practice.explanation: Use 'out of' to move from inside a building to outside.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: Go along the river to the park.
practice.answer: Go along the river to the park.
options: Go along the river to the park.
Go across the river to the park.
Go past the river to the park.
practice.explanation: Along means following the side of the river.

practice.prompt: The train goes inside the dark forest. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Our train went ___ the big forest.
practice.explanation: Use 'through' when moving inside trees or a tunnel.

practice.prompt: Match each preposition with its picture idea.
practice.explanation: Across crosses from side to side, past goes by, and towards goes in a direction.

practice.prompt: Do not stop at the library; keep going. Build the sentence.
practice.explanation: Go past means go by the library without stopping.

practice.prompt: The museum is on the other side of the park. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Go ___ the green park.
practice.explanation: Use 'across' to go from one side of the park to the other.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: Go straight on towards the museum.
practice.answer: Go straight on towards the museum.
practice.explanation: Towards shows the direction you are going.

lessons.title: If we miss it
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Omar are hurrying to catch a connecting train and making backup plans.

items.text: If we miss it we will
forms: if we miss it we will
items.example: If we miss it we will take the next train.
items.note: Use 'If we miss it we will' to explain your backup plan if you are late for a train.

items.example: We will be late unless we run now.
items.note: Use 'unless' to mean 'if not'—for example, 'unless we run' means 'if we do not run'.

items.example: I will text you as soon as we get to the hotel.
items.note: Say 'as soon as' for the exact moment one thing finishes and the next thing starts.

items.example: Take a warm coat in case it gets cold.
items.note: Say 'in case' when you prepare something now for a possible problem later.

items.example: We will catch the train as long as it is on time.
items.note: Say 'as long as' to mean 'only if' this one condition happens.

items.example: I will take it if there is a window seat.
items.note: Use 'I will take it if' when you agree to a ticket or seat on one condition.

grammar.title: First conditional and time words
grammar.explanation: After 'if', 'unless', 'as soon as', 'in case', and 'as long as', use the present simple tense—never 'will'. Put 'will' in the other part of the sentence for the future result.
examples: If we miss it we will wait at the café.
I will call you as soon as the train stops.

practice.prompt: The train leaves in two minutes! What happens if you are too late?
practice.answer: If we miss it we will take the bus.
options: If we miss it we will take the bus.
If we miss it we took the bus.
As soon as we miss it we sleep.
practice.explanation: Use 'If we miss it we will' plus the future plan.

practice.prompt: Listen, then choose what you heard.
practice.audio: We will miss the train unless we hurry.
practice.answer: We will miss the train unless we hurry.
options: We will miss the train unless we hurry.
We will miss the train in case we hurry.
We will miss the train as soon as we hurry.
practice.explanation: Unless means 'if we do not hurry'.

practice.prompt: Omar packs an umbrella even though it is sunny now. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: Take an umbrella ___ it rains later.
practice.explanation: Use 'in case' when you prepare for something that might happen.

practice.prompt: Match each linking phrase with its meaning.
practice.explanation: Unless means if not, as soon as means immediately when, and as long as means if.

practice.prompt: Smarty wants a cheap ticket. Build his sentence.
practice.answer: I will take it if it is cheap.
practice.explanation: Use 'I will take it if' to state your condition.

practice.prompt: Mia promises to message you right when her plane lands. Complete the sentence.
practice.text: I will text you ___ we land.
practice.explanation: As soon as means immediately after the plane lands.

practice.prompt: Say the sentence aloud. You can try again.
practice.text: We will be fine as long as we stay together.
practice.answer: We will be fine as long as we stay together.
practice.explanation: As long as sets the condition for being fine.

lessons.title: Lost and found
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Lily are at the station reporting a lost suitcase and a missing key.

items.example: Excuse me, I have lost my blue suitcase.
items.note: Say 'I have lost' when you cannot find something that belongs to you.

items.example: Help! I have been robbed on the platform!

items.example: My phone is missing. Where can I report it?
items.note: Ask 'Where can I report it?' to find the right desk or police officer to tell about a problem.

items.example: It happened when I was getting off the train.
items.note: Use 'It happened when' to explain the exact moment a problem took place.

items.example: Do not worry, I have a spare key in my coat.
items.note: A 'spare key' is an extra key you keep in case you lose your main key.

practice.prompt: Lily cannot find her passport anywhere. What does she say?

lessons.title: Trip diary
lessons.scenario: Smarty and Tom sit in the train carriage sharing stories about a big mountain trip.

items.example: We got lost in the forest because we had no map.
items.note: Say 'We got lost' when you did not know where you were or which way to go.

items.example: The train was delayed, so it took hours to get home.
items.note: Say 'It took hours' when a journey or walk lasted a very long time.

items.example: In the end, we found a friendly driver who helped us.
items.note: Use 'in the end' to tell how a long story or problem finally finished.

items.example: The best part of our trip was swimming in the lake.
items.note: Say 'the best part' to share your favourite moment from a trip.

items.text: I have never been so tired
forms: we have never been so tired
items.example: After climbing the mountain, I have never been so tired!
items.note: Say 'I have never been so tired' when you feel more tired than ever before.

items.example: Look at the mountains and the sea—what a view!
items.note: Say 'What a view!' when you see a really beautiful place from a window or hill.
